items.abstract: Abstract Shanidar Cave has long featured in debates concerning Neanderthal cognitive capacity and behaviour, including evidence for care and intentional burial. By identifying additional individuals, including Shanidar A reported here, new excavations have expanded a burial cluster first identified in 1960. Shanidar A, an older adult, was deposited around 75,000 years ago, decayed, and their skeletal remains were subsequently disturbed by a flash flood. Our findings raise the minimum number of individuals in this unparalleled cluster to five, supporting interpretations of complex, potentially meaningful Neanderthal mortuary behaviour. Shanidar A also demonstrates major non-fatal trauma to the face and rare evidence of perimortem penetrating trauma among Neanderthals. Trauma among Middle and Upper Palaeolithic Neanderthals and modern humans, and subsequent survival, is common. However, the facial injury was severe and unusual. It suggests care from group members, the evolutionary origins of which are also contentious. The nature of the perimortem penetrating traumatic injury adds to a small corpus of such injuries in the hominin fossil record. The morphology of this scapula perforation is consistent with injury from a wooden spear, providing valuable (albeit indirect) evidence for the use of wooden implements in the Middle Palaeolithic, which is often difficult to demonstrate given the rare preservation of organic materials.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Ardea alba</jats:italic>
                    (Linnaeus, 1758) is widely distributed, yet knowledge of its ocular morphology remains limited. This study described the morphometry and morphology of the eyeball and its accessory glands in six specimens using radiography, morphometry, light and scanning electron microscopy, and 3D scanning. The eyeballs showed similar descriptive morphometric values in the right and left eyes, accounting for approximately 11.2% of head mass and 12.12% of total skull length. The eye was classified as the flat type, a morphology previously associated in the literature with diurnal birds, featuring a yellow iris and a circular pupil. The scleral ring consists of 14 bilateral type A ossicles associated with hyaline scleral cartilage. Histologically, the cornea showed a well‐defined Bowman's membrane, and the retina had 10 distinct layers. The pleated type pecten emerged from the optic nerve and extended toward the vitreous body. The accessory glands were characterized as follows: the Harderian gland (type II) was the most developed; the lacrimal gland was “hockey‐stick” shaped; and the nasal gland (salt gland) was supraorbital in location and pyramidal in appearance. These results provide a robust anatomical basis for comparative avian ophthalmology.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Iara Fernanda Lima do Espírito Santo
Julia Vaz Feio, Max Alex Santos Ferreira, Iara Fernanda Lima do Espírito Santo, Elane Guerreiro Giese, Érika Branco, Antônio Basílio Guerreiro Junior, Ana Rita de Lima

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Interglobular dentin (IGD) has been used as a biomarker for vitamin D deficiency (VDD) in past populations. However, an evidence‐based threshold for the levels of serum vitamin D associated with IGD occurrence has not been established. Here, we explore the association between perinatal serum vitamin D levels, presence of IGD, and biological sex in the deciduous teeth of modern children from Otago, New Zealand. Ground sections were created from the deciduous central or lateral mandibular incisors of 54 five to 6‐year‐old children (27 M, 27 F) with known perinatal blood vitamin D levels. Vitamin D levels at birth were classified as deficient (≤ 30 nmol/L), insufficient (> 30mn/L–< 50 nmol/L), or sufficient (≥ 50 nmol/L), and scanned slides were scored blind by two observers for IGD presence or absence. Thirty‐seven individuals (68.5%) exhibited IGD. The distribution of IGD was similar across vitamin D levels considered deficient (35.1%), insufficient (32.4%), and sufficient (32.4%), with no significant association between IGD presence and vitamin D status (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.97) or IGD presence and sex (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.77). Our findings do not support an association between IGD formation in deciduous teeth and vitamin D levels at birth. The prevalence of IGD across the sample, particularly in secondary dentin, suggests IGD may represent a normal developmental feature. However, it is important to note that cord blood vitamin D levels do not reflect the individual's vitamin D status during the entire period of deciduous incisor formation. Further longitudinal clinical research is required to better understand the relationship between VDD and the formation of IGD.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Anne Marie Sohler‐Snoddy, Stephanie Chan, Rebecca Weastell, Victoria Chen, Benjamin J. Wheeler, Deanna Beckett, Carolina Loch
